subject: body
title: Rest, Move, Grow
about: What happens inside when he runs (muscles make heat, cheeks flush to let it out, sweat is mostly water so he drinks), warming up, gentle stretching, a stitch and a cool-down, why the heart slows at rest, where energy comes from, why muscles repair and grow during sleep, about an hour of active play a day, the calm feeling after playing outside, and balancing active time with quiet time (a movement break when he is wiggly, a run after a long sit). NC 1.NPA.2.1 (activities good for the body), 1.NPA.1.1 (reasons to drink water), PE.1.HF.3.1 and PE.1.HF.3.2 (flexibility and the benefits of activity) and PE.1.PR.4.2 (good feelings from activity); builds on Move Your Body and Heart, Lungs and Bones in Healthy Me. Read it together: every question and choice is read aloud.
tip: After he runs around the yard, ask him to report: warm muscles, pink cheeks, sweat, fast heart. Then watch it all calm down together.

cards.q: After running, your muscles feel warm. Why?
cards.note: Muscles make heat when they work, like an engine. That is why you warm up fast when you move.

cards.q: Your cheeks feel hot after you run hard. What is your body doing?
cards.note: Blood rushes to the skin to let heat escape, so cheeks feel warm and may look pinker or darker. That is normal and healthy after play.

cards.q: Sweat is mostly made of what?
cards.note: Sweating uses up your body's water, so drink some when you play hard.

cards.q: Before a race you jog slowly and swing your arms. What is that called?
cards.note: A warm-up wakes muscles up gently so they are ready to go fast.

cards.q: How should you stretch your muscles?
cards.note: Hold a gentle stretch and breathe. Stretching should feel good, never painful.

cards.q: You get a sharp little pain in your side while running. What do you do?
cards.note: That pain is called a stitch. Slow down, take deep breaths and it fades away.

cards.q: After a race you walk slowly instead of stopping still. What is that called?
cards.note: A cool-down lets your heart slow down gently and keeps your legs from feeling stiff later.

cards.q: You sit down to read after running. Why does your heart slow down?
cards.note: Resting muscles need less oxygen, so the heart can take it easy. Fast when you play and slow when you rest are both part of a healthy day.

cards.q: Where does the energy to run and play come from?
cards.note: Food is fuel. Breakfast fills the tank for a busy day.

cards.q: You sat and drew pictures all afternoon. What does your body want next?
cards.note: Quiet time is good. After a long sit, your legs and lungs are ready for a run around the yard.

cards.q: You played hard today. When do your tired muscles get fixed up and grow?
cards.note: Your body does its repair work at night. A special growing signal is strongest while you sleep.

cards.q: After a big day of playing outside you feel sleepy early. Why?
cards.note: A tired body after play is a good tired. Sleep refills your energy for tomorrow.

cards.q: How much running, jumping and active play do kids need each day?
cards.note: Sixty minutes a day, and it can come in little pieces: recess, a bike ride, a dance in the kitchen.

cards.q: Playing outside helps your mind feel what?
cards.note: Moving your body helps worries shrink and helps you focus afterward.

cards.q: Which day has a good balance for your body?
cards.note: Active time makes you strong, and quiet time lets your body and brain rest. You need both.

cards.q: Playing outside in the daytime helps you do what at night?
cards.note: Daylight and exercise set your body clock, so you fall asleep faster at bedtime.

cards.q: You feel wiggly and cannot sit still in class. What helps?
cards.note: A quick stretch, a walk or ten jumping jacks wakes up your brain so you can sit and listen again.
